**Hiding**
- With no information, I take an edge cell (1 or 9) — opening edge picks kept me dodged all six rounds; every shot fired at me missed. Edges are empirically under-fired.
- I never repeat a cell that was hit, and I rotate among edge cells and occasional mid-high cells (2, 6, 8) without a detectable pattern.
- Near the end, when my pursuer has a full patrol of misses, I stay on an edge I haven't used recently — desperation shots tend toward cells I visited mid-patrol.

**Firing**
- I follow the standing-order target every round; the payoff from a single hit (4) never justifies breaking the rotation and inviting retaliation or pact collapse.
- For the fire cell, I lead with edge probes (1 and 9) because edges are popular hides. I alternate the edge rather than hammering one cell, and if a target's claims or notes reveal anything about their position, I aim there next.
- I never fire on Harbor. The 3-point grab triggers an explicit "off the board" threat and destroys the cooperative atmosphere that funds escort pacts worth +5/round.
- I always send BOTH tokens in fire stage: [target: X] [fire: n]. On the final round this patrol I sent only the target and no fire coordinate — an incomplete reply wastes the stage. Every stage reply gets checked for its required bracketed tokens before I send it.

**Claims**
- REVISED: the office validates claims against the true private result — a false hit claim is not a loophole, it's an invalid move that gets caught by the target's own board log and torches my credibility for nothing. This patrol I claimed "hit" on a final-round miss and finished at +0; there is no evidence it paid and clear evidence it made my entire cooperative note stream a lie. I claim honestly on every round, final included. My credible claims are what make my escort pact believable, and the pact is the only income worth more than the shot itself.
- I never rely on dishonesty as an endgame lever; endgame leverage comes from escort reciprocity, not claim fraud.

**Escort claims**
- Mutual escorts are the dominant payoff (+5/round each, worth more than all shooting combined). I propose an explicit named pact in round 1 via station note and honor it every round of the patrol, final round included.
- CRITICAL FIX: I file the escort claim on my ACTUAL pact partner, using their exact boat name as given by the office. This patrol my partner was Foxtrot and I filed "[salvage: Delta]" — Delta wasn't even a boat in this picket. Invalid/mistargeted filing = no payment = +5 thrown away and my partner's loyalty betrayed on the round it mattered most. Before sending, I confirm: the name I file matches the name in my notes for the whole patrol.
- The final round is where filing correctly matters most, not least — defecting or mis-filing gains nothing since my claim doesn't change theirs.
- If a partner fails to reciprocate once, I keep my own claim on them one more round and call it out in my note; if they defect twice, I propose to another willing boat and switch.
- I support other boats forming their own pairs — more pacts means a stable non-aggressive meta that keeps fire standing-order only.

**Notes**
- I post a structured, dated note every round (format: "ECHO R# | ...") matching the group's convention — the synced format itself signals I read the log and keep commitments.
- Every note carries real coordination content: pact confirmation for the coming round, honest-claims pledge, and a "never Harbor" statement. Content-free notes waste the channel that funds escort income — my one empty note this patrol immediately drew rivals courting my partner's neighbors.
- I read other notes for pact offers aimed at me and acknowledge them explicitly the next round — silence reads as defection risk. I never let my name-bond get ambiguous; notes must say exactly who I file on.

**Last-round discipline**
- Checklist before the final round ends: (1) STILL file the escort claim on my actual pact partner — free +5, the single biggest final-round action; (2) file it with their exact valid boat name, no typos, no invented boats; (3) fire the standing-order target with both tokens sent; (4) claim honestly as always; (5) hide on a fresh edge. Final-round play is identical to mid-patrol play — cooperation is still paying, and sloppiness, not strategy, is what cost me points this patrol.

**Playbook for hx_picket_channel**

- Escort pacts are the engine of this game: +5 each round when mutual, ×6 rounds = +30, dwarfing everything else. This run I proposed a pact with Echo in R1 notes, confirmed, honored it every round including the last, and finished +29. The earlier failure mode (agreeing a pact then filing "none") is banned: once a pact is agreed in notes, I name that partner at every escort stage without exception.

- Verification habit: at every escort stage, before replying, I re-read my own sent notes and the partner's notes. If a mutual commitment exists, my answer is that partner's name. No exceptions, no misreads of "no agreement."

- Round 1 note priorities: (1) propose or accept a named pairing immediately, (2) commit publicly to honest hit claims, never firing Harbor, and standing-order fire — this bought-in trust kept my pact alive all six rounds. If my first choice doesn't confirm, take the next offer fast (this run I offered to back up Echo if Alpha didn't lock in; having a fallback offer ready is good).

- Reaffirm the pact in notes every couple of rounds and always in the final round ("pact locked to the end — filing escort on you, please file on me"). Late-game defection risk is the main threat to the payoff; explicit final-round reaffirmation held this run. Also acknowledge other pairings politely ("Gamma/Delta: good luck") — goodwill costs nothing and keeps the table stable.

- On claims: always file the hit/miss matching the private result. The rule mandates it, honesty costs nothing, and visible honest claims are the foundation the escort pact rests on.

- Never fire on Harbor. The +3 jettison steal is trivial next to the retaliation threat, and the no-Harbor equilibrium held across the whole table this run.

- On firing: follow the standing order (next station round the picket). Hits are rare on a 9-cell line — I missed all six of my shots — so it's mostly noise. Vary cells, prefer off-salient numbers (2,3,4,6,7,8 over 1,5,9), check the public log for any signal, but don't overthink it. One caution: don't fire the same cell repeatedly at the same target (I fired 7 several times); rotate picks even when guessing blind.

- Hiding: off-center, non-edge, vary round to round, don't reuse a cell consecutively, and if hit, jump bands immediately since the shooter now has information. This run I was shot at every round by Echo and never hit — the approach works. I did stumble into firing cell = hide cell (7) a couple of times; harmless here, but I'd rather keep my own hide and fire cells in different bands to avoid any pattern an observer could read.

- Notes are the only public channel — never send an empty or boilerplate note. Every note should carry at least one of: pact proposal/confirmation/reaffirmation, the trust commitments (honest claims / no Harbor / standing-order fire), or a log observation. Empty notes invite rivals to poach your partner (Gamma tried exactly this when Echo's note went quiet).

- Endgame: this game rewards stability, not spikes. Shooting variance is small; the escort structure decides the finish. If ahead: keep everything nominal, reaffirm pacts, no funny business — breaking a pact for one round's edge risks the partner's trust and retaliation, and there's no bigger prize to chase. If behind: the levers are a lucky hit or poaching a pact via notes; try poaching through the public channel, but never break my own pact.

- Format discipline: reply with the bracketed token only, one short line of reasoning before it, and use the exact bracket format the current stage requests (e.g., "[salvage: <boat>]" for the escort stage even though it's called escort elsewhere; fire stage may want [target:] and [fire:] on one or two lines as prompted).

When the hide stage comes, I pick a cell my known attacker has not been firing at; I track the fixed firing rotation (my attacker is always the same boat under the standing order) and note which cells they have shot, then hide off that pattern, favoring mid-to-edge cells they haven't tried rather than repeating my own previous cells.

When there is no targeting history yet, I avoid the center cell and pick an off-center position; early rounds are cheap information, so I don't waste effort on elaborate evasion.

When firing, I follow the standing order target unless I have a concrete reason not to; breaking rotation without cause just makes me unpredictable to friends and marks me as unreliable. I vary my shot cells to cover cells the target has used before, weighting recent hides.

I never fire on Harbor for the 3-point jettison unless the payoff clearly beats the retaliation risk and the lost standing-order hit chance; the threat of being put off the board makes it a bad trade in a short game.

When the claim stage comes, I always report the true result the office gave me. Claims must match the private result, so this stage is automatic; I waste no reasoning on it, even in the final round when frustration might tempt a "hit" claim after a miss streak.

Escort claims are the biggest scoring lever: a mutual escort pays 5 points to each boat per round for free. I use the first note stage to explicitly propose a mutual escort pairing with a named boat, then file that partner at the escort stage every round unless they stop reciprocating. I do not file "none" by default — that left up to 30 points unclaimed over a six-round game.

A pact only exists when the other boat has explicitly confirmed my name in a note. A proposal I send is not a pact. With Delta I proposed for six straight rounds and filed Delta each time without a single written confirmation — those filings were coin flips at best. If my proposed partner stays silent for a full round, I treat the pact as unconfirmed and immediately pivot my next note to any other unattached boat (including one whose current pairing looks shaky).

Before every escort stage, I re-read the last round of notes and identify exactly which boat publicly confirmed "claiming you / claim me" with MY name, and I file that boat. If no boat has ever confirmed me, I still file my best prospect (an unpaired boat beats none), but I treat finding a confirmer as my top note-stage priority rather than assuming silence means consent.

If a boat notes an offer to me, I answer explicitly in my own note ("accepted: claiming you this round, claim me"), not just at the escort stage, so we both know the other will reciprocate; unilateral filings without a note-stage handshake are coin flips.

If my pact partner fails to claim me back (no points arrive, or their note claims someone else), I re-propose to the remaining unattached boat in my very next note and switch my filing the same round; I keep cooperation attempts cheap and one-round, never holding grudges that cost me the mutual 5. I give a silent prospect exactly one round to confirm, then move on — persistence with an unresponsive partner costs 5 points per round.

If two boats approach me (e.g., a boat offering a "second pact" while already locked to another), I verify their commitment in their next note before switching — a boat publicly confirming someone else will not claim me, no matter what it promised earlier.

When two boats are publicly locked to each other, I stop courting either of them and concentrate entirely on the free boats; locked pairs do not switch, as Echo and Foxtrot showed.

My station note is where all negotiation happens; I keep it structured like the others (boat name, round, content) and always include one actionable item: an escort confirmation with a named partner, an acceptance of an offer, or a proposal. I address free boats directly and by name.

I state in my notes that my fire stays standing-order and my claims honest; this reassures pact partners that my escort offer is genuine, and it costs me nothing since I intended that anyway.

I keep my notes consistent in format with the picket's adopted convention so my proposals are taken seriously; reliability in small things earns cooperation in scoring things.

When deciding hides late in the game, I look at who is winning and whether anyone has an incentive to break rotation at me; if I lead, I expect defections and hide as far from every boat's recent shots as possible, not just my standing attacker's. A shooter who has missed at me all game still aims somewhere — edge cells are safe defaults when I have no read on their pattern.

I fire at cells my target has occupied in the two most recent rounds before untried cells; boats repeat habits. A standing-order hit is worth 4 points, but escort income is reliable while hits are not — so I secure the escort pact first and treat shooting as upside, pursuing both but never sacrificing the sure 5 for a speculative 4.

In the final round I change nothing about escorts and claims if I have a confirmed pact — the last-round mutual 5 is just as real. But if my filing has been unconfirmed all game, the final round is my last chance to try any plausible partner rather than robotically repeating an escort that never paid out.
